title: In England, the Progressive-Traditionalist Debate Is Back On
author: Andrew Old
summary: Old argues that England has become the shining example of traditionalist education, built on a knowledge-rich curriculum, orderly classrooms and strict behaviour enforcement, and that new Education Secretary Lucy Powell's agenda threatens that standing. He expects the long-running philosophical debate between traditional and progressive education to return to the centre of policy discussion. The post explains why the debate is hard to conduct, citing accusations of straw men and false binaries, and defends targeting the broad themes of progressive literature. It sets out a promise to detail the policy changes to watch in the next post. The move is to frame the debate and defend the existence of its terms before the substantive policy analysis.
points: England's education system has risen on a knowledge-rich curriculum, orderly classrooms and strict behaviour enforcement, according to Old.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell's stated priorities, including oracy parity and reimagined childhood, have reignited the traditional versus progressive debate.
Debating educational philosophy is difficult because critics are accused of misrepresenting opponents even when examples exist.
Progressivism is defined by its broad themes: criticism of adult authority, methods other than explicit instruction, and curricula that do not specify knowledge.
Progressives who lose ground on what to teach can shift to how to teach, so critics must identify the full array of themes.
quotes: England has become the shining example of traditionalist education. England has been riding high on the back of a knowledge-rich curriculum, a preference for desks in rows, and top inspection grades for some of the schools that do most to enforce the rules.
A major change in policy now may put England’s world-leading status at risk.
Discussions of educational philosophy are hard work because it is so important to engage with the ideas of those you disagree with.
Advocates of the ideology that has, for more than 100 years, been known as progressive education often resort to obfuscation to defend it against criticism.

It is necessary to target the criticism of adult authority, the promotion of teaching methods other than explicit instruction, and the support for curriculums that do not emphasise, and often do not specify, the knowledge to be taught.

If we do not identify the full array of progressive themes, then progressives can simply change their focus whenever they lose ground. If they are losing the debate about what to teach, then they can argue over how to teach.
My approach is simply to describe, from my own perspective, what debates we can expect.
